topics.title: Rule-of-law backsliding and constitutional-court capture: the Polish Constitutional Tribunal crisis and its wider European implications
topics.framing: In late October 2026 a judge elected by parliament in March 2026, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, ordered the suspension of Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice President Bartłomiej Sochański, prompting police deployment at the Tribunal, a crowd breaking the Tribunal gate, and the president cutting short a trip to hold crisis consultations. Former Tribunal presidents issued a statement calling for a path out of the crisis, the European Commission said parliament has the right to appoint judges and pointed to ECtHR interim measures of 5 May 2026, and the Commission's July 2026 Rule of Law Report recorded continuing problems with the Tribunal, execution of judgments and disputes over newly elected judges. Commentators also note contested appointments made by the Tusk government, including that of minister Maciej Berek, which polling suggested many Poles saw as politicising the judiciary.
topics.mainstream_view: The crisis is a rule-of-law problem in which a captured or delegitimised constitutional court blocks the execution of European judgments and undermines judicial independence; the remedy lies in restoring a court that meets European standards, with the Commission, ECtHR interim measures and the annual Rule of Law Report as the proper external anchors, and with parliament's appointment power treated as legitimate when exercised within that framework.
topics.global_south_view: The episode shows that 'rule of law' conditionality is applied unevenly and can itself become an instrument of political contestation, with competing camps each claiming constitutional legitimacy and external European institutions picking winners; the deeper question is who gets to define constitutional fidelity, and whether the vocabulary of capture is used selectively against some governments while comparable politicisation by others passes with milder comment.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides agree the Tribunal is in crisis and that judicial independence matters, but they diverge sharply on whether the EU institutions are neutral arbiters or selective participants in the political struggle.

topics.title: Climate/environmental justice through trade and investment law: the EU-NZ FTA climate complaint and France's fossil-fuel advertising ban
topics.framing: On 29 September 2026 the Dutch environmental justice organisation Both ENDS lodged the first environmental and climate complaint under the European Commission's Single Entry Point, alleging that New Zealand has broken the climate commitments in its FTA with the EU; the TSD chapter commits both sides not to lower environmental protections and retains their right to regulate. In parallel, France's partial ban on fossil-fuel advertising is being examined for its European implications, including proportionality, freedom of expression, internal market freedoms, the correct legal basis for EU action, and cross-border enforcement difficulties.
topics.mainstream_view: Trade agreements can be made to serve environmental goals through enforceable sustainable-development chapters and civil-society complaints, and the EU-NZ complaint is a test of the EU's fidelity to the rule of international law and of the credibility of mutual commitments; the French ban is a legitimate public-interest measure whose extension requires careful calibration against expression and internal-market freedoms.
topics.global_south_view: Sustainability chapters remain weakly enforceable, discretionary and asymmetrical, with enforcement channelled through a Commission-controlled entry point rather than binding adjudication, and with the risk that environmental standards become a further layer of conditionality imposed on trading partners while the EU's own consumption patterns go unaddressed; advertising restrictions, meanwhile, are a welcome check on corporate climate disinformation but must not become a pretext for market-fragmenting regulation.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides welcome using trade and advertising law for climate ends, but they differ on whether the EU's sustainability enforcement architecture is genuinely binding and even-handed or discretionary and asymmetric.

topics.title: Collective enforcement of international judgments and accountability for Russia: Council of Europe proposals on ECtHR award payments
topics.framing: On 30 September 2026 PACE adopted Resolution 2678 (2026) and Recommendation 2315 (2026) endorsing, for the first time in Council of Europe history, concrete proposals to secure payment of ECtHR just-satisfaction awards against a state unwilling to pay, following Russia's exclusion from the Council of Europe in March 2022 and its later withdrawal from the ECHR and from the anti-torture convention. Related debate concerns whether frozen Russian central bank assets could be used to satisfy such awards, with questions raised about countermeasures, reversibility and collective enforcement under international law.
topics.mainstream_view: Russia's non-payment and treaty withdrawals leave victims without remedies, and the PACE proposals are a proportionate, rule-of-law-preserving innovation that closes an enforcement gap while keeping the response within the framework of the Convention system and general international law.
topics.global_south_view: Using frozen sovereign assets or collective enforcement mechanisms to satisfy judgments sets a precedent that could later be turned against weaker states, stretches doctrines of countermeasures and collective enforcement beyond what international law sustains, and risks substituting political sanctioning for neutral adjudication.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides accept that Russia's non-compliance is a real enforcement failure, but they divide on whether collective asset-based enforcement is a principled repair or a precedent with uneven and potentially coercive downstream effects.

topics.title: Decentring Eurocentric constitutionalism: African constitutionalism, 'confluence constitutionalism', and liberal constitutionalism beyond the West
topics.framing: A Verfassungsblog focus argues that African constitutionalism should be read not only as reception but as legal translation, in which international norms are adapted rather than simply received, and proposes a research agenda for endogenous constitutionalism rooted in African social, political, cultural and historical realities. Companion posts describe liberal constitutionalism as a tradition whose global history is one of circulation and transformation rather than one-way diffusion, with the Global South as a site of production as well as implementation.
topics.mainstream_view: Liberal constitutionalism remains a coherent tradition with universal purchase, and its globalisation is best understood as diffusion, adaptation and circulation in which comparative scholarship can identify shared standards while acknowledging local variation.
topics.global_south_view: The framing of 'beyond the West' must go further than circulation talk: the task is decolonising comparative constitutional law, theorising alternatives in their own normative terms, and treating colonial legacies and linguistic divides as central rather than as background context.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides reject crude diffusionism and accept transformation through circulation, but they differ on whether liberal constitutionalism remains the reference point or must itself be decentred and replaced by endogenous normative vocabularies.

topics.title: International criminal justice under pressure: US sanctions against the ICC, Duterte before the ICC, and evidentiary/normative thresholds (Yekatom)
topics.framing: The United States announced sanctions against the ICC in October 2026, prompting debate over whether the objection to territorial jurisdiction amounts to an 'except the USA' carve-out from foundational rules, and over possible EU use of a blocking statute and its effects on commercial actors. In parallel, the Duterte case in The Hague is being analysed as both a legal proceeding and a site of memory and accountability politics in the Philippines, while a Yekatom prosecution response raises questions about the content of a 'normative' threshold.
topics.mainstream_view: The sanctions are an attack on the rule of law and on rules the US itself helped build, and the appropriate response is to defend the Court's jurisdiction and the equality of states before the law, while refining evidentiary and normative standards so that prosecutions remain rigorous and credible.
topics.global_south_view: The Court's authority is undermined both by great-power coercion and by its own selective practice; the Duterte case shows that accountability also happens through testimony, memory and domestic mobilisation beyond The Hague, and that legal findings matter chiefly insofar as they support reparations, institutional reform and victims' political voice.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides defend the Court against US sanctions, but they diverge on whether the central threat is external coercion or the Court's own selectivity and its distance from affected communities.

topics.title: Platform work, labour rights and the EU Platform Work Directive: 'employees without employers' and algorithmic management
topics.framing: The EU Platform Work Directive introduces a rebuttable presumption of employment where facts indicate control and direction by a digital labour platform, shifts the burden of proof to the platform, and imposes transparency and human-oversight requirements for automated monitoring and decision-making; member states face a December 2026 transposition deadline. Verfassungsblog notes that the presumption alone will not solve the problem, since delivery platforms have interposed 'fleet partners' between themselves and workers, and that algorithmic-management provisions apply to all platform workers regardless of employment status.
topics.mainstream_view: The Directive is a milestone that rebalances bargaining power through a rebuttable presumption, burden-shifting and algorithmic transparency, and the priority now is timely and consistent transposition across member states so that the level playing field and legal certainty the Directive promises are realised.
topics.global_south_view: The presumption is easily circumvented by subcontracting chains and intermediary 'fleet partners', leaving workers formally employed by entities with no real employer function; without addressing fragmented employer structures and enforcement capacity, the Directive risks becoming a symbolic milestone rather than a substantive improvement in working conditions.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides treat the Directive as significant and both flag implementation risk, but they differ on whether the remaining problem is transposition timing or a structural evasion built into platform business models.
